article.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification / claude.dev Blog
article.text:
Engineering
How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
AUTHOR
Addy Osmani
CATEGORY
Engineering
PUBLISHED
Nov 16, 2026
READING TIME
10 min
On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude. At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important.
Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel.
That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems.
What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens.
You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again.
So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team.
NOT ALL TESTS ARE CREATED EQUAL: 3 TESTS WORTH INVESTING IN
No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid.
If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes.
Now, here are the three types of tests I think are most worth investing in.
E2E tests
If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page.
The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you what’s broken.
FIG AA unit test may show “Error: Timeout after 30 seconds,” but an end-to-end test can show a screenshot with a description of what’s broken.
While unit tests are faster and less flaky, it’s possible to pass them and still break the feature. This is because both the agent and the test don’t understand the full task.
With E2E tests, it is effective to give your agent hands and eyes on the real running system. You can use a skill to boot, drive, and inspect the app with tools like CDP, simulators, or API harnesses.
The feature map can serve as a guide and grading rubric for agents as they typically list features from the user’s point of view with descriptions of paths, keyboard shortcuts, selectors, and expected results.
Property tests: constraints that can’t break
A lot of tests are based on what you thought might go wrong. Property tests look at the edge cases that people tend to miss, which is where agents often fail.
You start by writing a statement you think can’t fail and then use a test library (fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, proptest for Rust, etc.) to generate…

article.title: Introducing FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 — RUNTA
article.text:
Introducing FrontierHarness Eval v1.1
November 17, 2026·14 min read·Shilin Zhu
agentsharnessevaluationbenchmarkharbor
TL;DR
We partnered with Baseten to build the largest-scale harness leaderboard using 83B tokens across 27,280 agent runs. We wanted to answer two questions: when you switch your model, should you consider switching the harness too? What is the best harness for each model?
Previously, our v1.0 FrontierHarness leaderboard ranked harnesses on a single model, Kimi K3.
V1.1 expands the benchmark to 22 harnesses × 5 models × 62 tasks × 4 attempts, 76× the size of v1.0.
Through our experiments, we found that you should consider switching harnesses when switching models to maximize your experience.
Each model had a different best-value (pass rate vs. cost) harness: Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Oh My Pi with Muse and Alma with Kimi-K3. Cost ranks moved far between models.
By cost per task, the median harness moved 11 of 22 places, and Codex CLI went from 1st with GLM-5.3 to 16th with Kimi-K3.
Result
Figure 1. Cost per task and pass rate of each harness
Each point is one harness: further left is a lower average cost per task, and higher is a higher pass rate. The orange line joins the harnesses that no other harness beats in both cost and pass rate. Select a model to filter all figures of this post.
Over all models, four harnesses are on the line: OpenCode v2 (lowest cost per task, $0.561), Pi, Codex CLI and ZCode (highest pass rate, 61.9%). The others cost up to 1.6 times as much and passed 50.6% to 60.2%.
Each card names the best-value harness for one model: the lowest cost per pass, unless another harness costs at most 30% more per pass and passes at least 5 points more often. This rule picked ZCode over OpenCode v1 with DeepSeek (25% more cost, 7.7 more points) and Alma over Oh My Pi with Kimi-K3 (9% more cost, 6.5 more points).
Why We Built FrontierHarness Eval v1.1
V1.0 ran nine harnesses with one model. Their pass rates were within 17 points of each other, but the median cost per pass differed by 17 times. We thought that this came mostly from the pair of harness and model: a harness that is cheap with one model can be expensive with another.
V1.1 runs each harness with five models.
What We Tested
Harnesses. 18 harnesses. The four DeepSeek Harness profiles have different tool sets, and OpenCode ran at two versions. Each counts separately: 22 configurations. Table 2 in the appendix gives their versions.
Models. Baseten served all five: GLM-5.3 (zai-org/GLM-5.3), GLM Flash (zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash), DeepSeek (deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017), Muse (meta-models/muse-spark-open) and Kimi-K3 (moonshotai/Kimi-K3).
Tasks. 62 terminal tasks. The time limits are those of the tasks, from 15 minutes to 8 hours.
Setup and Scoring
Configuration and Runtime
We ran the Harbor evaluation with each harness’s default settings, because we think this is closest to how people use a harness every day. Each harness used the same version and settings with all models, at the maximum reasoning effort.
Figure 2. How Harbor and Runta divide the work in each trial
Each trial gets a new Runta runtime, which is deleted at the end. Thus no trial can see the files of an earlier trial.
Scoring Method
Table 1. Methodology
A cell is one harness and model pair. We use the two cost metrics of our dashboard:
Average cost per task: the mean cost of the priced trials of each task, then the mean over the tasks. Figure 1 and the cost ranks use it (Figures 4 and 5).
Cost per pass: the average cost per task divided by the pass rate. The best-value harness uses it (Figures 3, 6 and 7).
We pick the best value by cost per pass because we want harnesses at the top left of a chart of pass rate against cost per task: a high pass rate at a low cost. Draw a line from the origin to the point of a harness. Its slope, pass rate ÷ cost, is the passes per dollar. Cost per pass is the inverse of this slope, so the…

MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash: two new coding models built for the everyday enterprise coding tasks, delivering leading performance at a fraction of the cost of competing models.
Performance and speed for everyday coding
MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance for common enterprise coding tasks and excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multi-file implementation, repo wide reasoning, and UI. It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost.
Meanwhile, MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume work such as code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost.
Production quality at less than half the price
To deliver the best price-performance, we’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work.
Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the cost.1
MAI Code 2 is also tuned for producing great dashboards and visualizations, and excels at visual coding. In blind frontend app evaluations, reviewers preferred its results over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time.2
In addition, MAI Code 2 Flash offers comparable performance to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the cost, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks.3
Beyond coding
MAI Code 2 is also becoming the workhorse behind Microsoft products. From Code 2 Flash we further optimized a single model, MAI Work Flash, to serve multiple Microsoft products across M365 and Fabric IQ.
Excel: Our model is on par for accuracy and token efficiency with GPT 6 Luna across key internal Excel customer-scenario benchmarks.
PowerPoint: On key production benchmark scenarios that measure frequent PowerPoint tasks, our model performs on par with GPT 6 Luna in both quality and token efficiency.
Word: Our model performs similar to GPT 6.1 sol (while being significantly smaller) on 5 key internal benchmarks using ~42% fewer input tokens per call than GPT6.1 Sol in production.
Teams: Our model beats GPT 6 Luna at tracking decisions, filling knowledge gaps, and adapting custom instructions using up to 28% fewer tokens on instruction following and tool calling.
FabricIQ: In offline evaluation runs our MAI model outperforms GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-6-astra, and Opus-5.5 at DAX query generation, the core capability behind “Chat with your Data” for Power BI semantic models.
Get started
MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are available in GitHub Copilot, and Code 2 Flash is in limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry. Soon, we’ll be releasing it on Open Router, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo.
Learn more about customizing MAI Code 2 on our Custom Models page.
About these results
Results reflect evaluations on specific coding tasks and configurations. Performance and cost comparisons vary by workload, model configuration, reasoning effort, and pricing assumptions.
MAI Code 2 performance and price: All models were run at max reasoning effort. DeepSWE 1.1, TerminalBench 2.1 and SWE Atlas were run on MSBench (Microsoft’s internal eval platform) with the GitHub Copilot CLI without subagents. FrontierCode 1.1 scores and costs are from Artificial Analysis; MAI-Code-2 cost is shown at its 50% promotional price.

article.text:

JetBrains IDEs Transformed for the Agentic Era of Development – With Air
Dominique Rolink
As agents write more code, individual productivity goes up, but the bottleneck moves to review. 49% of developers now spend four or more hours a week reviewing AI output and correcting prompts (Atlassian State of Developer Experience Report 2026). We believe this means you need to understand what changed, decide whether it belongs in your codebase, and be able to maintain it after the session ends.
This is why we shipped Air in JetBrains IDEs, with the 2026.3 release. This allows you to bring your coding agents into your existing development environment, with one place to track their progress, review their changes, and send feedback. It is a major step in making JetBrains IDEs more agentic, while still respecting classical workflows, where the developer remains in control and at the center of everything.
Air is more than a new place to chat with AI. Because it runs inside the IDE, it brings IDE code intelligence to you and your agents. Through the IDE’s MCP server and built-in skills, agents can check inspections, run your build and run configurations, query your databases, and use the IDE’s own refactorings. In IntelliJ IDEA and CLion, they can also drive the debugger.
Try Air in Your IDE
In this post: Key features of Air | Coming from AI Assistant | Free AI | FAQ
Key features of Air in JetBrains IDEs
Parallel agent sessions, worktrees, and notifications
Follow sessions across projects in one place to understand which agents are working, which need your input, and which have unread results. Notifications tell you when an agent needs you. Give each agent its own local Git worktree so that parallel sessions don’t collide, and review its changes as with any other session. Worktrees that agents create on their own aren’t tracked in Air yet, but we’re working to make this a reality.
Start sessions from presets
Save the agent, model, and instructions you use for a type of task as a preset. Start a new session from it instead of setting everything up again, and keep separate presets for different use cases.
Your existing agents and subscriptions are supported
Air works with agents such as Junie, Codex, Claude Agent, and GitHub Copilot, and connects to other compatible agents through ACP. Bring compatible agents already installed on your machine or add them from the registry, then choose your model and connect your subscription.
Depending on the setup, that can mean your existing provider subscription, an API key, or JetBrains AI. A paid JetBrains AI subscription is not required.
You can also use your Claude Pro or Max subscription with Claude Code in Air’s terminal surface, which opens as a full-screen IDE tab.
Reviewing agent code and Code Notes
You do not have to write every line to own it, but you do need to understand it. When an agent finishes, open the review panel to see what the session changed, then use the IDE’s own tools to check it: navigate the code, run inspections and tests, or use the debugger. Leave Code Notes on specific lines to request changes or ask questions, and send them back to the session with the code context attached.
Code Notes also work with Air’s terminal agents, so you can review their outputs in the IDE and steer the next iteration without giving up your terminal workflow.
IDE intelligence for you and your agents
Supported agents can use native JetBrains IDE capabilities, including debugging, profiling, database management, and semantic code search. You retain access to the exact same tools to inspect and verify their work.
Code completion and next edit suggestions
Code completion keeps working in the editor as before, and it does not count against your JetBrains AI quota. Next edit suggestions work with Air when you sign in with a JetBrains…

article.title: An update on our recent security incident · Cursor
article.text:
Blog / company
Nov 13, 2026·company
An update on our recent security incident
6 min read
On October 29, we shared that we were investigating a security incident and a malicious, unauthorized copy of Anthropic's Claude Code extension that appeared in the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace. After an extensive investigation over the past two weeks, we want to share more context on the attack and the related impact.
The vast majority of customers were not affected, and we have contacted each affected customer directly with the details that apply to them.
Protecting the safety of our customers' data is a core priority we take seriously. This incident involved data we stored and shared, credentials we issued, and systems we operate. We are addressing the impacts and are enhancing our security measures based on what we have learned.
#What happened
Our investigation has pieced together the following picture:
It started at Fireworks. An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks. The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them. That bucket contained limited coding agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions not in Privacy Mode, which we were permitted to use for model training. A small number of those traces contained credentials that had not been redacted; less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed. Starting with those credentials, the attacker reached select SaaS tools used by Cursor. From these tools they accessed select archived non-production Cursor source code repositories (some containing business contact information), limited customer support data and email conversations, product usage metrics and contact details, summaries of some coding agent conversations, and some credentials users had sent to the Cursor support team.
Our monitoring systems identified the unauthorized activity. After becoming aware of the unauthorized activity, we deactivated the vendor's key, opened an incident response workstream, and began revoking and rotating credentials and hunting for any further unauthorized access. As we identified further access, we cut it off. Out of an abundance of caution, we temporarily disabled internal and product services well beyond what the evidence required, which temporarily disrupted certain Cursor features. We restored each one once it was safe to do so.
The attacker published a malicious extension. On October 29, using a stolen credential from the exposed data from our internal system, the attacker placed malicious, unauthorized copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace. Anthropic did not publish this copy, and this was not a vulnerability in Anthropic's product. The marketplace source, Open VSX, never had the malware. At most 5,000 users who requested specific cached versions of the extension on October 29 potentially received the malicious build. It was available for approximately 11 hours before we removed it. We took it down, took the extension marketplace offline, and worked with the cloud service provider hosting the attacker's server to take it down.
We notified customers. On October 30, we published a security notice on our blog and on X with indicators of compromise, remediation steps and scripts to check your system, and began notifying affected users and team admins through in-app notices and email. If credentials were exposed, we emailed team admins a list of the specific keys to rotate, and asked the third-party services that issued those credentials to revoke them. If customer support or business data may have been involved, we notified customers directly. hn.title: Launch HN: StarSling (YC P25) – Self-improving CI for agent-volume repos
hn.text:
We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling (https://starsling.dev), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows.
Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost.
Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762.
I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill.
We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww.
Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents:
- Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry
- Propose an optimization
- Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change
- Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant
- Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence
We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time:
- https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs (12.8x)
- https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck (5.5x)
- https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot (3.9x)
- https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh (11.7x)
- https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu (36.4x)
Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this: https://github.com/starslingdev/skills. The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself.
We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly (https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks).
We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent: https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks.
To try it, give your agent this URL: https://docs.starsling.dev/start. You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes.
Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here: https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge.
We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup!

comments.author: colek42
comments.text:
We should probably be measuring deployable merges to main. The math just doesn't work for pipeline based CI as you add more agents.
Three things matter.
1 -- How many non-conflicting changes can actually be made at one time (Fan Out)
2 -- How long a critical path takes
3 -- How many times you have to run that critical path. Most orgs run it 2-3x, once before the PR in the agent loop, once in CI, and another in the MQ
This is why most orgs cant get past about 12 PRs an hour.
